cards.title: Landing page conversion math and what the 20% claim means
cards.summary: Conversion rate = form fills ÷ page views; use it to judge and rank landing page variants.
cards.use_when: Setting up measurement for a paid-ads landing page or PDP-equivalent lead page so you can tell if a page is winning before spending more on traffic.
steps: Define conversion as the completed primary action (form submit or tracked call), not a page view or scroll.
Calculate conversion rate as conversions ÷ landing page sessions, expressed as a percentage. Example: 10 form fills from 100 sessions = 10%.
Segment by traffic source (Google Ads, SEO, Facebook) because the same page can convert differently by medium.

Treat the source's headline numbers as one operator's experience, not a benchmark: he reports his best page hit ~20% versus a typical worldwide 2–4%, and that his leads converted to paying customers at 6–8% depending on medium. Those are single-business results with no verified methodology, so use them to illustrate the gap between landing conversion and purchase conversion, not as targets.
Before optimizing copy, confirm the denominator is right — if you count views but not submits (or vice versa) you will 'improve' a page that never changed performance.
caveats: Purchase conversion rate and form conversion rate are different metrics; a 20% landing conversion can still yield 6–8% paying customers.
No statistical significance method is given in the source — pair with a proper test design before declaring a winner.
cards.source_name: Claude Code Website Masterclass_ How I Got 20% Conversions (10x The Average).docx

cards.title: Judge design as binary trust, not beauty
cards.summary: Website aesthetics only need to clear a trust threshold; ugly pages still convert if the offer and proof are strong.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much budget and time to spend on visual design versus copy, proof and offer for a store or lead landing page.
steps: Assess the page against one question: does a first-time visitor trust this enough to keep reading, or does it look like a scam?
Note the source's claim that first impressions form in roughly 50 milliseconds — this is his stated figure, not a verified study you should quote as fact.
If the page clears the trust bar, redirect design time to copy, social proof, offer and speed instead of pixel-polish.
Use free design references (the presenter uses dribbble.com) to lift the baseline look when you lack a designer, then move on.
Apply the same test to product pages: a clean, credible PDP with strong photos and proof will usually beat a heavily designed page with weak proof or unclear offer.
caveats: The presenter still says good design increases conversion rate — it is simply not the primary lever. Do not use this as an excuse for a broken or dated-looking page.
Trust thresholds vary by category; a fashion store's aesthetic expectations differ from a B2B lead page.
cards.source_name: Claude Code Website Masterclass_ How I Got 20% Conversions (10x The Average).docx

cards.title: Write less: control the 10% visitors actually read
cards.summary: Cut landing page copy so the headline and a few supporting lines carry the message; hide the rest for SEO.
cards.use_when: Editing a landing page or product page whose copy feels like a wall of text and where visitors bounce before reaching the CTA.
steps: Assume visitors read roughly 10% of your copy; the presenter's stated behavior is that people see the headline, subheadline, 2–3 bullets and maybe one more line.
Because you cannot control which 10% they read if everything is visible, deliberately choose what stays above the fold and in the main flow.
Strip any sentence that does not either establish credibility, state the outcome, or move the reader toward the form/CTA.

For pages you want to rank in Google, keep long-form text for SEO but place it inside accordions/dropdowns so the page stays visually short for readers while the words remain indexed. The presenter cites 1500+ words as a common SEO landing page target — treat as a heuristic, not a rule.
Rewrite remaining copy around benefits (time saved, money earned, pain avoided, peace of mind, status, freedom) rather than features or tech stack.
caveats: The 10% read figure and the 1500-word SEO target are presented as the speaker's working heuristics; verify with your own scroll and engagement data.
Concise copy still needs specificity — cutting words is not a license to drop the actual offer or proof.
cards.source_name: Claude Code Website Masterclass_ How I Got 20% Conversions (10x The Average).docx

cards.title: Sell outcomes, let buyers rationalize with features
cards.summary: Lead with emotional benefits and keep features as supporting proof that buyers use to justify the decision afterward.
cards.use_when: Writing the offer block, hero copy or ad-to-page message for a store or service landing page.
steps: Identify the emotional benefit the buyer is really purchasing: saved time, more revenue, pain avoidance, peace of mind, status or freedom. The presenter uses a Ferrari as the analogy — nobody pays for leather seats, they pay for status and then justify it with build quality.
State the benefit in the headline or offer block, then use features (tools, process, materials, stack) further down as the rationalization layer.
Translate credibility assets into benefit language: 'top 1% of DJs out of 5,000' reads as peace of mind that the wedding won't be ruined, not a staffing stat.
Avoid leading with the tech or method you are proud of; the presenter notes builders love talking about their stack, but buyers don't care about it.
Test the same offer expressed as different benefit angles — the presenter says rotate and test promises rather than assuming one framing is right.
caveats: This is standard sales psychology asserted by the presenter, not an experiment he ran on benefit-vs-feature copy specifically.
Highly technical or regulated categories may require more feature detail up front for credibility.
cards.source_name: Claude Code Website Masterclass_ How I Got 20% Conversions (10x The Average).docx

cards.title: Strip navbar and footer from paid-ad landing pages
cards.summary: Ads-funded pages should have no navigation or footer so the only available actions are the form or the call button.
cards.use_when: Building or auditing a paid-traffic landing page where every extra click costs you acquisition budget.
steps: Remove the site navbar and footer from ad-funded pages so visitors cannot wander into About, Terms or blog pages.
Allow exactly two actions: submit the form or tap-to-call. Everything else is treated as leakage.
Place the form directly on the page — never behind a Contact page or a link. The presenter states this is mandatory because visitors bounce when they can't find how to reach you.
If a legal or required link must remain, keep it out of the primary visual path so it doesn't read as an option.
Logic to apply when arguing with stakeholders: if you paid $10 to acquire the click, an About page visit is $10 spent on something that will not produce a lead.
caveats: The source says this is exclusively for advertising pages, not SEO pages — SEO/organic pages may still need navigation and internal links.
Sitewide footers with legal or policy links may be required in some jurisdictions; confirm before removing.
cards.source_name: Claude Code Website Masterclass_ How I Got 20% Conversions (10x The Average).docx

cards.title: Place CTAs throughout the page and pin one on mobile
cards.summary: Distribute CTAs so the visitor can act the moment they're ready, and use a persistent bottom bar on mobile.
cards.use_when: Laying out CTAs on a landing page you're building or reviewing, especially after checking mobile rendering.
steps: Sprinkle CTAs down the page rather than relying on one button at the end, so a visitor who has read enough can act immediately.
Keep the desktop and mobile treatments different — the presenter explicitly calls this two devices, two rules.
On mobile, use a single CTA pinned to the bottom of the viewport so it stays visible while scrolling, and have it jump straight to the form.
Check the mobile version with browser developer tools: three dots → More tools → Developer tools → responsive/device mode, then switch between iPhone, tablet and desktop widths.
Have every CTA land on the form or call action — not on a section, accordion or secondary page.
caveats: The source gives no CTA density number; add as many as read naturally without breaking the page's flow.
Too many competing CTA labels can dilute the primary action — keep one action with consistent wording.
cards.source_name: Claude Code Website Masterclass_ How I Got 20% Conversions (10x The Average).docx

cards.title: Founder video: sell yourself, not the service
cards.summary: A short founder video on the page can lift landing conversion substantially; keep it under ~45 seconds and make it about trust.
cards.use_when: Adding or evaluating a video block on a landing page, PDP or about-the-brand section to raise trust with first-time visitors.
steps: Shoot a roughly 45-second video where you sell yourself — who you are, that you're real and trustworthy — not a service explainer. The presenter reports his own page went from 10% to 15% conversion when he added one, framing that 5-point gain as 33% more leads. That is his single-business result, not a benchmark.
Structure the video: quick intro, some social proof, results, three reasons to choose you, a call to action, and optionally a risk reversal (e.g. money back in the first week).
Don't sell features or list services; the goal is that the viewer can see, like and trust the person they'd be working with.
Production values are low-stakes — the presenter rented a co-working space on a Saturday for the background. Expect to film many takes; he says it may take 50 tries.
If your video is bad, it can hurt conversion (his stated view), so review it before publishing rather than shipping the first take.
caveats: The 10%→15% (33% lift) figure is the presenter's own reported result with no test details; treat as a directional anecdote.
A 45-second cap is his guidance, and he admits his own video ran longer; longer can work but risks losing attention.
cards.source_name: Claude Code Website Masterclass_ How I Got 20% Conversions (10x The Average).docx

cards.title: Show a portfolio when the product is judged visually
cards.summary: For visually judged work, an absent or weak portfolio can block the inquiry entirely — treat it as close to binary.
cards.use_when: Designing the proof section for a store or service page where the buyer must approve the look of the output (photography, furniture, custom goods, interiors).
steps: Ask whether the buyer can tell they'll like the result without seeing examples. If not, portfolio becomes a gating requirement rather than a nice-to-have.
Show a curated set of work that matches the specific intent of the page or ad — photography examples for the shoot type, not a general gallery.
Keep examples high quality: the presenter describes portfolio quality as near-binary, where a bad portfolio can lose the lead before any contact happens.
Place the portfolio where the visitor will naturally look for it in the evaluation flow rather than buried at the bottom.
If the catalog itself is the proof (ecommerce), make sure the visible product imagery on the PDP does the same job as a portfolio: it must let the buyer confirm they like the output.
caveats: The source explicitly says portfolio is not required for every business — it applies where the deliverable is visual and taste-dependent.
No conversion numbers are given for portfolio; this is a qualitative judgment from the presenter.
cards.source_name: Claude Code Website Masterclass_ How I Got 20% Conversions (10x The Average).docx

cards.title: Turn FAQ into an objection-handling block
cards.summary: Use FAQs to answer whatever is actually stopping people from converting, sourced from real sales conversations.
cards.use_when: Building or rewriting the FAQ section on a landing page or PDP, or when form submissions are low despite good traffic.
steps: Ask yourself what stops a visitor from filling out the form or buying: price, business model, unclear process, timing, guarantees.
Harvest objections directly from calls with prospects — the presenter says to explicitly ask whether anything felt ambiguous, and they will tell you.

Write the FAQ answers to dissolve those specific objections, not to fill space. The presenter calls the default 'I don't know what to put so I'll add text' approach useless for conversion (only useful if you're padding for SEO).
Update the FAQ as new objections repeat in sales calls, so each new batch of visitors gets the answers the last batch needed.
Keep FAQs discoverable but collapsed, consistent with the general 'less visible text' principle.
caveats: The source gives no measurable lift for FAQ changes; it's presented as a probable conversion contributor.
If FAQ text exists purely for SEO, keep it — that's the one exception the presenter allows.
cards.source_name: Claude Code Website Masterclass_ How I Got 20% Conversions (10x The Average).docx

cards.title: Make the phone number a click-to-call on mobile
cards.summary: A tappable phone number captures high-intent visitors who want an answer now, not a form response later.
cards.use_when: Adding contact options to a mobile landing page where some visitors are in immediate-need mode rather than research mode.
steps: Place a clickable call action on the page — not just a displayed number — so a mobile visitor can be on the phone within seconds.

Apply the presenter's reasoning about intent: callers are in 'get it done now' mode, not planning mode, so a call may convert at a higher rate than a form. He states he is unsure of the exact comparative stat and is reasoning from psychology, and cites a Google-sourced claim he doesn't fully trust.
For attribution, buy distinct phone numbers per page or campaign so you can tell which page generated the call.
Use a VoIP number (the presenter mentions Twilio, or numbers bought through your CRM) so work calls are separated from personal and are callable from computer or app.
Route the call to a live human quickly — the source's speed-to-lead section targets connecting within about 10 seconds.
caveats: The presenter explicitly flags the 'phone converts higher' claim as his own speculation, not a stat he verified; test it in your own business.
Per-page phone numbers add cost and management overhead; weigh against the value of attribution.
cards.source_name: Claude Code Website Masterclass_ How I Got 20% Conversions (10x The Average).docx

cards.title: Video testimonials: 30-second self-shot clips as primary proof
cards.summary: Ask clients to record short phone-video testimonials; the presenter credits nine of them with cutting cost per conversion from $200 to $30.
cards.use_when: Building the social proof section for a store or service page when written testimonials alone feel unconvincing.
steps: Reach out to real clients and ask for a genuine 30-second testimonial recorded on a phone — explicitly low production, no studio.
Aim for a set of several testimonials; the presenter used nine on his photo/video business.
Expect and accept that many visitors won't watch them — the presenter's argument is that the mere presence of video proof raises peace of mind.

Prioritize video over written testimonials. The presenter says he personally distrusts written testimonials, suspects AI-generated ones and stock photos, and treats video as the credibility anchor; written ones are better than nothing if video isn't available.
If using written reviews as a fallback, pair them with external review sources so they're not fully self-published.
caveats: The $200→$30 cost-per-conversion result is the presenter's own reported campaign result from a separate Google Ads account; it is an anecdote, not a promised outcome.
Filming testimonials requires client cooperation and time; expect it to take real effort, which the presenter acknowledges.
cards.source_name: Claude Code Website Masterclass_ How I Got 20% Conversions (10x The Average).docx

cards.title: Write case studies with specific before/after numbers
cards.summary: Specific, quantified case studies outperform vague ones, especially for B2B pages.
cards.use_when: Writing case-study or results sections for a B2B store, agency, or service landing page.
steps: Replace vague outcome statements with a before-and-after number: conversion rate went from 3.1% to 19.4%, revenue increased by X over Y period.
Include a time frame so the result is contextualized rather than implied as permanent.
Show multiple case studies where possible — the presenter's example page had additional case studies ready to expand.
Explain the mechanism: the presenter's stated logic is that specific results let the buyer 'future pace' — imagining the same outcome for themselves.
Keep the case study tied to an outcome the buyer cares about, not internal process detail.
caveats: The example numbers (3.1% → 19.4%) come from the presenter's sample page; do not reuse them as benchmarks.
The source says case studies are strongly recommended for B2B and not necessarily required for B2C.
cards.source_name: Claude Code Website Masterclass_ How I Got 20% Conversions (10x The Average).docx

cards.title: Borrow authority with brand logos, review badges and trust stats
cards.summary: External credibility markers — logos, third-party review badges, and countable trust stats — raise trust with modest effort.
cards.use_when: Filling out the trust row of a landing page or PDP where the buyer has no prior relationship with the brand.
steps: Add logos of companies you've genuinely worked with (the presenter lists TD, Microsoft, McLaren and Samsung) to borrow their authority.
Add external review badges (e.g. Trustpilot) because the review process is outside your control, which increases perceived credibility.

Note the presenter's observation that a perfect 5.0 rating can read as suspicious — either no reviews or filtered — and that 4.7–4.9 often looks more believable. This is his opinion, not a tested finding.
Add 'trust stats' — years in business, number of events/projects completed, revenue generated, number of reviews — as concrete counters.
Place these markers where they'll be seen early, not only in the footer.
caveats: Only display logos and stats you can substantiate; the presenter's list is his own client history, not a generic example.
Trustpilot or equivalent badges require maintaining that profile — don't show a badge you can't back.
cards.source_name: Claude Code Website Masterclass_ How I Got 20% Conversions (10x The Average).docx

cards.title: Offer formula: verb + metric + time frame + risk reversal
cards.summary: Frame the offer as a concrete promised outcome with a deadline and risk removal, and adapt when the outcome can't be quantified.
cards.use_when: Drafting or A/B testing the main offer block on a landing page or PDP.
steps: Write the offer as: 'We will [verb] your [metric] by [number] in [time frame] — or [risk reversal].' Example shape: 'We'll generate 20 leads per month or your money back.'
Use the formula where the outcome is concrete and measurable (leads, sales, bookings). The presenter states it fits best when you sell leads, sales, or something hyper-specific.

When the result isn't easily quantified — his example is landscaping — fall back to the buyer's real desires. For a wedding DJ he wrote: top 1% of DJs out of 5,000 (credibility), we remove planning stress so you can have fun (benefit).
Add a risk reversal: money back in the first week, or a pay-you-to-show-up incentive as the presenter used on an agency offer.
Rotate and test different promise framings rather than committing to one — the presenter says he is actively split testing offers.
caveats: The formula is the presenter's own generalization from what he read and used; not every category has a quantifiable metric.
Risk reversals must be operationally manageable — don't promise refund terms you can't honor.
cards.source_name: Claude Code Website Masterclass_ How I Got 20% Conversions (10x The Average).docx

cards.title: Speed-to-lead: automate routing so reps call in seconds
cards.summary: Route form submissions into a dialer instantly via webhook so the sales rep connects within roughly 10 seconds.
cards.use_when: Setting up lead handling behind a landing page, especially when paying per click and racing competitors to the prospect.
steps: Connect your form submission to a webhook that pushes the lead into your VoIP dialer immediately.
Target a connection time of about 10 seconds between form submit and a rep being on the call — the presenter calls this speed-to-lead and describes it as a massive non-negotiable.
Keep the phone number clickable on the page as the parallel fast path for visitors who'd rather call.
Use VoIP instead of personal phones (Twilio or your CRM's telephony) so routing, tracking and work/life separation are built in.
Instrument both paths — form fills and calls — in your tracking so you can compare which produces leads and paying customers.
caveats: No conversion lift numbers are given for speed-to-lead in this section; it's asserted as high-impact, so verify in your own funnel.
Twilio and CRM telephony interfaces change frequently; verify current setup steps before implementing.
cards.source_name: Claude Code Website Masterclass_ How I Got 20% Conversions (10x The Average).docx

cards.title: Mobile-first audit with browser device mode
cards.summary: Check every landing page at phone and tablet widths before launching, since the presenter claims most traffic is mobile.
cards.use_when: Running a pre-launch QA pass on a landing page or PDP layout.
steps: Open the page in a browser and enter developer tools: three dots → More tools → Developer tools → responsive/device toolbar.
Switch between iPhone, tablet and desktop presets, and also drag the responsive handle slowly to catch awkward breakpoints between standard sizes.
Check specifically that the sticky mobile CTA is visible and functional throughout the scroll, that the form is usable one-handed, and that content doesn't overflow.
The presenter cites device splits of roughly 64% mobile, 3% tablets and 33% desktop; treat these as his figures, not universal, and confirm your own analytics.
If a breakpoint looks broken, iterate on the layout until phone, tablet and desktop all render acceptably.
caveats: Device split percentages vary by industry; check your own analytics rather than adopting 64/3/33.
Browser developer tools interfaces change; the exact menu path may differ.
cards.source_name: Claude Code Website Masterclass_ How I Got 20% Conversions (10x The Average).docx

cards.title: Fix page load speed with Lighthouse, not guesswork
cards.summary: Pull the Lighthouse report and hand it to an AI agent to fix the flagged performance issues, iterating until the score is high.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing a slow landing page or PDP that may be losing conversions to load time.
steps: Run Lighthouse inside browser dev tools (three dots → More tools → Developer tools → Lighthouse) to get performance, SEO, accessibility and best-practices scores.

The presenter cites a study claiming 1-second loads convert around 3.05% and that every extra second roughly halves conversion — treat as a cited study, not your own data, but it justifies treating speed as a priority.
Identify the common culprits he names: images, videos and large graphics.
Copy the Lighthouse diagnostics and paste them into your AI coding agent with a prompt like 'here's the Lighthouse report, optimize for page load speed and for desktop, tablet and mobile'.
Re-run Lighthouse after changes (the presenter's example went from 90% to 95%) and repeat the copy-paste-fix loop until the score reaches the level you want.
caveats: The conversion-vs-load-time figures are cited from an unspecified online study; do not treat 3.05% or the halving per second as a guaranteed rule for your store.
Lighthouse scores measure technical performance and don't capture real user experience on slow networks.
cards.source_name: Claude Code Website Masterclass_ How I Got 20% Conversions (10x The Average).docx

cards.title: Build a reusable landing page skill to multiply pages
cards.summary: Package your page structure into a repeatable generator that produces city×service landing pages on demand.
cards.use_when: Scaling from one winning landing page to many local or service-variant pages for SEO or ads.
steps: Use the 'zipper' approach: one side is the city or region (e.g. Toronto, Vancouver, Manhattan, the Bronx), the other is the service (tree trimming, landscaping, snow removal).

Create a page for each meaningful city×service combination so the search result matches the query exactly — the presenter argues that searchers for 'tree trimming in Toronto' won't click a page about tree removal.
Make the headline and body specific to the same term the visitor searched, so ad or SERP → page → follow-up message → sales call are all aligned to the same keyword.
Encode the winning structure into a skill/workflow (the presenter uses a Claude Code skill named something like '/landing-page-generator') that takes service, city and traffic source as inputs.
Ramp publishing gradually — the presenter warns against generating hundreds or thousands of pages at once because Google may penalize it; start slow and increase over time.
Keep a homepage as the root, with landing pages branching off for each combination.
caveats: The presenter explicitly warns that mass-generating pages can get you penalized; his guidance is to ramp gradually with no specified safe rate.
The tool invoked here (Claude Code inside Anti-Gravity) is subject to interface changes — verify current setup before relying on it.
cards.source_name: Claude Code Website Masterclass_ How I Got 20% Conversions (10x The Average).docx

cards.title: Expect nothing from a single page; get to 20% by testing dozens
cards.summary: High conversion rates come from running many variants and following the data, not from one perfect build.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to keep iterating on a landing page or to accept the current version and shift budget elsewhere.
steps: Accept the presenter's framing that nobody — not you, your friends, Claude or Google — can guarantee a 20% page; if it were easy, everyone would do it.

Plan to build and test many variants over time; the presenter says his 20% page followed testing roughly 40, 50, or 60 landing pages, which he describes as a one-time upfront investment paying off for years.

Set up a split-testing tool that randomly assigns visitors to variant A, B, C at roughly equal rates (the presenter uses PostHog; he notes Hotjar or Microsoft Clarity as alternatives) so you can compare which page produces the most form fills.
Rotate losers out and create fresh variants, then rerun the test — this is the loop, not a one-off.
Base decisions on the measured conversion rate (form fills ÷ visitors) rather than on how the page looks or how clever the copy seems.
caveats: The presenter demurs on how to definitively reach 20% — treat this as a process, not a promised outcome.
No significance thresholds or minimum sample sizes are given; adopt proper test design before declaring winners.
cards.source_name: Claude Code Website Masterclass_ How I Got 20% Conversions (10x The Average).docx

cards.title: Track conversions by routing submitters to a Thank You page
cards.summary: Use a dedicated Thank You page as the conversion event so PostHog (or any analytics tool) logs it reliably.
cards.use_when: Configuring conversion tracking for a landing page or any form-based funnel.
steps: Route every successful form submission to a dedicated 'Thank You' URL rather than showing an inline confirmation.
Configure your analytics tool to log a conversion whenever a visitor lands on that Thank You URL.
This sidesteps form-submit event complexities and keeps the conversion definition unambiguous, which is what the presenter recommends in PostHog.
Keep the Thank You page free of other links that might be mistaken for further steps — the funnel should end there.
Verify the tracking by submitting a test form yourself and confirming the conversion appears in your analytics.
caveats: Thank You URL-based tracking can miss conversions where users cancel page load; pair with server-side events where accuracy matters.
Analytics tool interfaces change; verify the current event setup in PostHog or your chosen tool.
cards.source_name: Claude Code Website Masterclass_ How I Got 20% Conversions (10x The Average).docx

cards.title: Use heatmaps and session recordings to find friction
cards.summary: Watch real visitors and see where they click to locate friction points, then fix the page based on what you observe.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing a page with traffic but weak conversion, when you need qualitative clues before running new variants.
steps: Install a heatmap and session-recording tool — the presenter names PostHog, Hotjar, Microsoft Clarity as options, and notes they're free-tier friendly.
Watch a sample of recordings of actual visitors scrolling and clicking on your landing page or PDP.
Use heatmaps to see which areas attract attention and which CTAs get ignored; combine with the headline/10%-read rule to decide what to cut.
Look specifically for dead clicks, rage clicks and drop-off points near the form or CTA.
Turn findings into new variants to test rather than making a single untested change.
caveats: No method is given for how many recordings to sample before drawing a conclusion.
Heatmaps show attention and clicks, not why a visitor acted — pair with direct customer questions before making big changes.
cards.source_name: Claude Code Website Masterclass_ How I Got 20% Conversions (10x The Average).docx
